title: 2 Kings 18:26–37
context: Hezekiah’s officials ask the Rabshakeh to speak in the Syrian language, commonly identified with Aramaic, rather than in the Jews’ language within earshot of the people on the wall. He refuses and shouts to the people directly, urging them not to let Hezekiah make them trust in the LORD, promising them a land like their own, and asking whether any of the gods of the nations delivered their lands from Assyria. The people keep silent as the king commanded, and the officials return to Hezekiah with their clothes torn. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat this as shared ground: the enemy’s propaganda aims to separate God’s people from trust in him, and the LORD is not one god among many. A parallel account appears in Isaiah 36.

verses.text: Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, Shebnah, and Joah, said to Rabshakeh, “Please speak to your servants in the Syrian language, for we understand it. Don’t speak with us in the Jews’ language, in the hearing of the people who are on the wall.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the officials asking the Rabshakeh to speak in the Syrian language so the people on the wall will not understand. They want to protect morale.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the request as wise leadership in a crisis. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing concern for the people’s fear.

verses.text: But Rabshakeh said to them, “Has my master sent me to your master and to you, to speak these words? Hasn’t he sent me to the men who sit on the wall, to eat their own dung, and to drink their own urine with you?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh refusing and speaking crudely of the siege’s horrors. His aim is to frighten the ordinary people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his coarse words as deliberate psychological warfare. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly as a picture of the suffering a siege brings.

verses.text: Then Rabshakeh stood and cried with a loud voice in the Jews’ language, and spoke, saying, “Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh shouting in the Jews’ language, calling the people to hear the great king. He bypasses the leaders entirely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the speech as a rival word set against the word of the LORD. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a contest over whose word the people will trust.

verses.text: The king says, ‘Don’t let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you out of his hand.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh warning the people not to let Hezekiah deceive them. He tries to drive a wedge between king and people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the accusation of deception as ironic, since the real deceiver is the one speaking. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as an attack on legitimate leadership.

verses.text: Don’t let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD, saying, “The LORD will surely deliver us, and this city shall not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh urging the people not to trust the LORD to deliver them. The deepest attack is on faith itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the taunt as directly defying the LORD, which the following chapter will answer (compare 1 Samuel 17:26). Both traditions commonly read the verse as the spiritual center of the speech.

verses.text: Don’t listen to Hezekiah.’ For the king of Assyria says, ‘Make your peace with me, and come out to me; and everyone of you eat from his own vine, and everyone from his own fig tree, and everyone drink water from his own cistern;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh offering peace and the comfort of each person’s own vine, fig tree, and cistern. Surrender is presented as safety.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the offer as a counterfeit of God’s promised blessing. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a temptation to trade faith for apparent security.

verses.text: until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive trees and of honey, that you may live and not die. Don’t listen to Hezekiah when he persuades you, saying, “The LORD will deliver us.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the promise of a land like their own, which really means deportation. The offer hides exile behind attractive words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as revealing the empty promises of those who oppose God. Both traditions commonly read it as a warning against being persuaded by appealing lies.

verses.text: Has any of the gods of the nations ever delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh asking whether any national god has delivered his land from Assyria. He places the LORD among the idols.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the question as the fatal error of treating the LORD as one god among many (compare Deuteronomy 4:35). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as the key boast the LORD will answer.

verses.text: Where are the gods of Hamath and of Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, of Hena, and Ivvah? Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh listing the gods of conquered cities, including Samaria. History seems to support his claim.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his inclusion of Samaria as ignoring that Israel fell because of its own unfaithfulness. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a misreading of history.

verses.text: Who are they among all the gods of the countries, that have delivered their country out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh asking why the LORD should deliver Jerusalem when no other god could. His arrogance reaches its peak.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the boast as setting up the LORD’s decisive answer. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as pride that goes before a fall (compare Proverbs 16:18).

verses.text: But the people stayed quiet, and answered him not a word; for the king’s commandment was, “Don’t answer him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people staying quiet as the king commanded. Silence can be an act of faithful restraint under provocation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the people’s obedience to Hezekiah as wise under provocation. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a refusal to argue with propaganda.

verses.text: Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, came with Shebna the scribe and Joah the son of Asaph the recorder to Hezekiah with their clothes torn, and told him Rabshakeh’s words.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the officials returning to Hezekiah with torn clothes and reporting the words. Grief and distress mark their report.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the torn clothes as a sign of mourning over blasphemy against God. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as leading Hezekiah to turn to the LORD.
